instructions: Compare each English claim, scope, evidence and triple against the cited source before filling decision. Accept, revise or defer; do not mark reviewed without doing the review. This file records author approval, separate from source checks.

records.comment: The claim and relation were checked against pp.73 and 72. Presenting Wau Kikik as a traditional Malay wau is explicitly documented, without inferring its date of invention.
The headings on pp.72 and 73 and the practice-section heading on p.144 were checked. The Kikik–Laga link is documented within each section’s scope, without assuming universal identity.
The name Wau Kaca and its explanation through powdered glass on the string were checked against pp.73 and 72. The glass concerns the string, not the kite body.
The reviewed book pages do not contain the name Wau Kemetek. It is retained as a candidate name within the assignment scope, without an asserted factual edge.
The statements on pp.73 and 72 identifying Wau Kikik as the official wau of Melaka were checked. The claim is restricted to the book’s 2002 publication context.
The statements on pp.73 and 72 enumerating three described types of Wau Kikik within the book’s classification were checked.
The first form’s head and dented/concaved description (berlekuk) were checked against pp.72 and 73, without assuming unspecified geometric dimensions.

The second form was checked in both languages. A tail is common to both accounts; the Malay and English shape descriptions are both retained as a difference in specification, without imposing one form.
The third-form descriptions on p.72 (segi empat tepat) and p.73 (perfect square shape) were checked. Both descriptions are retained as a difference in geometric specificity.
The characterization of Wau Kikik as the simplest design among traditional wau was checked against pp.73 and 72 and retained as the book author’s qualitative description.
The resemblance to Eddy Kite and its reported Western name Malay Kite were checked against pp.73 and 72, maintaining a strict distinction between resemblance and identity.
The explicit absence of a hummer/busur was checked against pp.72 and 73, with Wau restored at the start of the Malay quotation and the negation limited to the specified component.
The explicit absence of sobek carvings was checked against pp.73 and 72, without extending the negation to the coloured patterns visible in the kite images.
The explicit absence of the leaf-shaped wings common in traditional wau was checked against pp.73 and 72. The negation is restricted to the described wing shape.
The basic covering of layers of wau paper was checked against pp.72 and 73, without assuming a specific layer count or standard specifications.
The p.144 description of Wau Laga practice as more challenging than the single-string kite used in the comparison, requiring considerable skill, speed and concentration, was checked.
The competitive objective of breaking the opponent’s string and the defensive objective of protecting one’s own string from being cut were checked against pp.144 and 148.
The p.144 account of string normally glazed with fine powdered glass to cut the opponent’s string during competition was checked, preserving the qualifier normally and the historical context.
The p.144 statement describing Wau Laga as more popular on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia was checked and retained as a qualitative account in the 2002 edition.
The p.144 long-range launch involving two players was checked, including both pairs of role labels used in the text: juru anjong/juru main tali and juru lancar/juru tarik.
The p.144 distance between launcher and puller, 30–50 feet / 9–15 metres, was checked and restricted to the launch separation between the players.
The p.144 preparation and launch-coordination steps were checked: rolling up the remaining string to prevent tangling, the puller signalling the launcher, and releasing the string in stages.

The p.146 account of control difficulty when the kite is close to the player and the altitude condition of about 200 feet / 60 metres was checked, including its attribution to The technic of controlling Wau Laga.
The summary record linking string handling with stability and direction on p.146 and defensive slackening on p.148 was checked against the accompanying detailed records.
The opening sentence on p.144 presenting Wau Laga as another type of traditional Malay wau was checked and retained alongside the headings on pp.72 and 73.
The p.146 conditional action of pulling the string to restore stability when the kite moves too far in a particular direction was checked.
The p.146 guidance to prepare sufficient string in piles on the ground so it can be released easily if the kite starts diving sharply at low altitude was checked.
The first stage of directing flight during ascent on p.146, by releasing the string slowly, was checked and linked to the next conditional step.
The p.146 condition and result were checked: when the kite’s head points towards the desired direction, holding the string with one or both hands makes it move in that direction.
The p.148 statement identifying speed as the most decisive factor in the described competitive attacking situation was checked.
The p.148 account of the attacking manoeuvre, in which players compete to cross their kite string with the opponent’s string, was checked.
The wording on p.148 about the advantage of being positioned below the opponent was checked. Its precise spatial referent is not resolved without further evidence.
The p.148 defensive action of releasing the string quickly so it slackens when under attack was checked.
The p.148 explanation that slackening the string when defending makes it more difficult to cut was checked.
The conditional competitive relation on p.73 concerning defeat of the opponent’s wau upon contact with Wau Kaca during a competition was checked.
